editor_spans.body: The most telling line in this week's Ukraine material is not about missiles. It is the Prime Minister's remark to the Commons that 'on diesel, the quickest way to get it back onto world markets without rewarding the aggressor is an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks.' That links the UK's support for a reciprocal energy ceasefire to fuel prices at home as well as to protecting Ukrainian civilians. The ceasefire would bind both sides, so Kyiv would stop its own strikes on energy targets too. The government says it wants exactly that because those strikes keep diesel off world markets.

Read this way, the spokesperson's response to the US–Russia agreement makes more sense. It spends as much time on 'global energy markets', 'energy prices and the cost of living' and 'stable energy markets' as on Ukraine. It also never says what the agreement contains, and only 'fully supports US-led efforts'. London needs Washington's ceasefire to work for reasons of its own. That is why its public line treats Russian breaches as Moscow's failure, not Washington's: 'Russia had no interest in peace.'

The military figures are small next to the rhetoric of 'doubling down'. Of the £45 million missile package, £10 million is being brought forward, set against a £1.6 billion programme already committed over four years. The levers that would actually move Moscow are financial: the maritime-services ban on Russian LNG, which the Chancellor and Foreign Secretary are pressing partners to copy, and sanctions now covering over 90% of Russian oil-producing capacity. Britain's distinctive weight here comes from shipping and insurance, not from munitions.

Two announcements a day apart point in opposite directions. In Derby the government is merging the railway into one national body: GBR will 'bring the railway together around one mission', run from a single headquarters for up to 450 staff. In Lanarkshire the Prime Minister says the Scottish Government is too centralised and that power 'was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament'. Labour's case for decentralising applies to Holyrood. For the railway, which it controls directly, it prefers a single national body.

The Scottish 'offer' is also political. It is made through No10 North and the Scotland Office, the UK government's own outposts. It invites councils and regions in North Lanarkshire, Fife and the Highlands to deal with Westminster partly over the head of Edinburgh. Calling it 'two governments, one goal' does not hide that it sets up a second route to power that Holyrood does not control.

The railway claims deserve the same scrutiny. The fare freeze is credited to public ownership, but a freeze is a ministerial decision that any owner could be told to make. The 600 apprenticeships come to about 150 a year over four years. That is a modest number given that fewer than 7% of rail workers are under 25. The site work at Becketwell begins in 2027 and ends in 2029, after the next likely general election, so the HQ's main effect before then is symbolic.

The biggest news in the Commons statement is not about the UN. It is the Prime Minister's move from 'the summit' to 'a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term', with 'the British public will be the boss'. That wording leaves room for a future vote on the UK's place relative to the EU. He presents the 20 November package of food, emissions trading, energy linking and youth mobility as a first step towards that, not a final settlement.

The new Lord-Lieutenant of Tyrone has an honourable record: a career in the RUC/PSNI, Omagh District Commander on the day of the 1998 bombing, decades of welfare work for police widows. But every institution on his CV comes from one community's civic life: the RUC, the Presbyterian kirk session and the Royal British Legion. Tyrone's population has a nationalist majority, and the Crown's representative there is still drawn from the other tradition. That shows how little the lieutenancy has changed since the policing reforms of the Good Friday era.
